The integrand is radial, so use polar coordinates \(x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta\). The point \(r=0\) has measure zero, and the resulting polar integral is finite for large \(n\).

\[
I_n=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 
\frac{n}{r\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^3}\, r\,dr\,d\theta
\]

Cancel the factor \(r\) in the denominator:

\[
I_n
=2\pi\int_0^1 \frac{n}{\cos(\pi r)+n^2r^2}\,dr.
\]

Now scale \(u=nr\), so \(dr=du/n\) and \(r=u/n\). Then

\[
I_n
=2\pi\int_0^n \frac{1}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{n}\right)+u^2}\,du.
\]

Define

\[
f_n(u)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{n}\right)+u^2}, & 0\le u\le n,\\[1.2ex]
0, & u>n.
\end{cases}
\]

For each fixed \(u\ge0\), as \(n\to\infty\),

\[
f_n(u)\to \frac{1}{1+u^2}.
\]

We can apply dominated convergence. For \(n\) large, say \(n\ge12\):

- If \(0\le u\le 2\), then \(\frac{\pi u}{n}\le \frac{\pi}{6}\), so \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{n}\right)\ge \frac12\). Hence \(f_n(u)\le 2\).
- If \(u\ge 2\), then \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{n}\right)\ge -1\), so

\[
f_n(u)\le \frac{1}{u^2-1}\le \frac{2}{u^2}.
\]

Thus \(f_n\) is dominated by the integrable function

\[
g(u)=
\begin{cases}
2, & 0\le u\le 2,\\
2/u^2, & u>2.
\end{cases}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^\infty f_n(u)\,du
=
\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{1+u^2}\,du
=
\left[\arctan u\right]_0^\infty
=
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

Finally,

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} I_n
=
2\pi\cdot \frac{\pi}{2}
=
\pi^2.
\]

\[
\boxed{\pi^2}
\]
